files.lesson.md: --- order: 22 unit: networks node: AC9M10SP02 n1 uses: [AC9M8SP03 n1] connection: train-map title: Nodes and edges summary: "A network keeps only who is joined to whom. The dots are nodes, the lines are edges, and a node's degree is how many edges meet there. Lengths and positions on the page don't mean distance." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Pick up a train map and plan a trip. What can you read off it, and what can't you?" --- You're at Fernbank and you need to get to Hilltop. The map on the platform wall shows the stations as dots and the tracks as lines. Which stations can you reach without changing trains? ## A made-up train map ```step stage: info insight: "A made-up map with six stations lets students name nodes and edges before the lesson uses the words; Make comes back to it and adds a line." diagram: ref: diagrams.mmd#map alt: "A train map with six stations. Fernbank is joined to Quay. Quay is joined to Market and to Park. Market is joined to Hilltop and to Westgate. Westgate is joined to Park." caption: "A made-up train map" role: stimulus ``` Here's the map. It isn't a real city's: the stations are made up. Each line joins two stations you can ride between with no stop in the middle. Try the trip from Fernbank to Hilltop. Which stations do you pass through? ```code diagrams.mmd#map flowchart TD F[Fernbank] --- Q[Quay] Q --- M[Market] Q --- P[Park] M --- H[Hilltop] M --- W[Westgate] W --- P ``` ## Predict: two lines ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to which ride is longer, from how long two lines are drawn, shows who reads line length on a network as distance." check: type: predict q: "On the map, the line from Market to Hilltop is drawn about three times as long as the line from Fernbank to Quay. In real life, which ride is longer?" options: - "Market to Hilltop" - "Fernbank to Quay" - "You can't tell from the map" actual: "You can't tell. How long a line is drawn is whatever fits on the page. Fernbank to Quay could be 12 km and Market to Hilltop 1 km. The map only tells you which stations are joined." ``` Two lines on the same map, and one is much longer. Which ride would take you further? ## Run: read the map ```step stage: run insight: "Counting the stations reachable from Quay in one ride introduces degree without the word: it is a count of lines, not of kilometres." check: { type: number, q: "Each line is a ride with no stop in the middle. From Quay, how many stations can you reach in one ride? Then look back at your prediction.", answer: 3, explain: "Fernbank, Market and Park. Three lines meet at Quay." } ``` Count the lines that meet at Quay. Fernbank, Market and Park are all one ride away. ## Investigate: what the map keeps ```step stage: investigate insight: "A line on a network stands for a connection, not a length; the node's degree counts connections; Lena reads the length of a drawn line as the length of the ride." tasks: - check: type: question q: "On this map, what does one line stand for?" options: ["A track that joins two stations with no stop in between", "The distance between two stations", "The time a train takes", "A street you can walk along"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The map doesn't show distances. A short line and a long line can be the same ride.", "Times aren't on this map either.", "It's a rail line, not a street."] explain: "A line (an edge) says the two stations are joined. That's all this kind of map keeps." - check: { type: number, q: "A bus network has stops A, B, C and D, with routes A to B, B to C, C to D, D to A and B to D. What is the degree of B? Work it out on paper first, then type it.", answer: 3, explain: "B is joined to A, C and D, so its degree is 3." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lena" text: "Lena says the ride to Hilltop must take longest. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: network-scale-map explain: "Line 3: the drawn length of a line isn't the length of the ride. The map keeps which stations are joined, not how far apart they are." - check: { type: number, q: "Add up the degree of every station on the map. What do you get?", answer: 12, explain: "Fernbank 1, Quay 3, Market 3, Hilltop 1, Westgate 2, Park 2: that's 12. It's twice the 6 lines, because each line has two ends." } ``` ### What a line stands for Look at the line between Market and Hilltop. What is it telling you? ### Degree A network is made of **nodes** (the dots, here the stations) and **edges** (the lines between them). The **degree** of a node is the number of edges that meet at it. Here's how to read the map. ```worked 6 stations :: Each station is one node: 6 nodes. 6 lines :: Each line between two stations is one edge: 6 edges. \text{degree of Quay} = 3 :: Quay is joined to Fernbank, Market and Park. \text{degree of Hilltop} = 1 :: Hilltop is joined to Market only. ``` Now try one on paper. A bus network has four stops, A, B, C and D. The routes are A to B, B to C, C to D, D to A and B to D. Sketch it, then find the degree of B and type it. ### Find the mistake Read Lena's working. Which line says something the map doesn't? ### Add up the degrees Add the degrees up for every station, then look at the number of lines. ## Modify: change the map ```step stage: modify insight: "Adding a station and a line changes degrees by one; a station with no line still counts as a node, with degree 0; and a node you can't reach is not connected to the others." tasks: - check: { type: number, q: "The council adds a new station, Lakeside, joined by one new line to Hilltop. What's Hilltop's degree now?", answer: 2, explain: "Hilltop had one line, to Market. The new line makes two." } - check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: a new station, Marina, opens with no line to any other station yet. What's Marina's degree?", answer: 0, explain: "No lines meet there, so its degree is 0. It's still a node." } smaller: check: { type: question, q: "Marina has no line to any other station. How many lines meet at Marina?", options: ["None", "One", "Six"], answer: 0, explain: "None. Degree counts lines, so Marina's degree is 0." } - check: type: question q: "Can you ride from Fernbank to Marina?" options: ["No: no line leads to Marina", "Yes: Marina is on the map", "Yes, if you change at Quay", "Only at weekends"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Being on the map isn't enough: you need a path of lines to get there.", "Quay doesn't have a line to Marina either.", "The map doesn't show timetables."] explain: "A trip needs a path of edges. With no edge at Marina, there's no way to get there, so Marina isn't connected to the rest of the network." ``` ### Lakeside Hilltop had one line. What happens to its degree when a new line joins it? ### A station with no lines A station with nothing joined to it is still a station on the map. How many lines meet there? ### Getting to Marina For a trip, you need lines you can follow one after another. ## Practise: degrees and edges ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading degrees off a description, using that each edge has two ends, saying what a network doesn't show, and a review of 3D points." tasks: - check: { type: number, q: "In a network, A is joined to B, C and D, B is joined to C, and C is joined to D. What's the degree of C?", answer: 3, explain: "C is joined to A, B and D: degree 3." } - check: { type: number, q: "A network has 8 edges. Add up the degrees of all its nodes. What do you get?", answer: 16, explain: "Each edge has two ends, so the degrees add up to 2 × 8 = 16." } smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Each edge has two ends, and each end counts once towards a degree. How many ends do 5 edges have in all?", answer: 10, explain: "5 edges × 2 ends = 10." } - check: type: question q: "Which of these can you work out from a train map like this one?" options: ["Which stations you can ride between without changing trains", "How many kilometres from Quay to Park", "Which line is quickest", "Where the stations really are on a street map"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Distances aren't on the map.", "Times aren't on the map.", "The positions on the page don't match the real positions."] explain: "The map keeps connections only: which stations are joined." - check: { type: number, q: "Review: in 3D coordinates, P is (2, 3, 4) and Q is (2, 3, 9). How many units above P is Q?", answer: 5, explain: "Only the up value changes, from 4 to 9: that's 5 units." } ``` ### Degree ### Ends of edges ### What the map shows ### Review The third number of a 3D point is how far up it is. ## Make: add a line ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the train map and adding a line: updating the counts is easy; saying what the new line doesn't tell you is the idea." hint: ["The new line adds one edge.", "Each end of the new line adds one to a degree."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The council adds a new line joining Hilltop and Park. Work out how many lines are on the map now, and the new degree of Hilltop and of Park. Then say whether a rider can tell from the map if the new line is the quickest way from Hilltop to Park." steps: - ["$6 + 1 = 7$ edges", "one new line adds one edge"] - ["Hilltop: $1 + 1 = 2$. Park: $2 + 1 = 3$", "each end of the new line adds one to that node's degree"] - ["The rider can't tell", "the map keeps which stations are joined, not how long the ride is"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Why can't the rider tell if the new line is quickest?" options: ["The map doesn't show how far or how long a ride is", "Short lines on the map are slow", "The new line isn't on the map", "A map can only show one line at a time"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Line length on this map isn't a time. It could be fast or slow.", "It is on the map: you've just drawn it.", "Maps show many lines at once."] answer: "7" answerLabel: "Lines on the map now" feedback: - ["6", "The new line makes one more."] - ["8", "One new line adds one edge, not two."] criteria: - "I added one edge, because there's one new line." - "I added one to the degree at each end of the new line." - "I said the map doesn't tell the length or time of a ride." explain: "The map now has 7 edges. Hilltop's degree is 2 and Park's is 3. A rider can't tell from the map how long the new ride is." ``` Back to the train map. Work this out on paper first, then type the number of lines. **Also used in** - **Street maps and journey planners.** Each junction is a node and each street an edge, the idea behind the route you see on a phone. - **Next lessons.** Following a path along edges (Every street once), then solids drawn as networks (Euler's rule). ```teacher summary: Students read a made-up train map as a network (nodes, edges, degree), see that the drawn length of a line isn't a distance, and update the counts when a line is added (AC9M10SP02, node 1). time: 35 timing: Opening and Predict 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 6 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can name the nodes and edges of a network and say what each one stands for. - I can find the degree of a node. - I can say what a network diagram keeps and what it leaves out. struggle: Reading the drawn length of a line as a distance. Ask what the line would look like if the same two stations were drawn on a different page. before: > The stations (Fernbank, Quay, Market, Hilltop, Westgate, Park), the bus stops and every number are made up. A real city's train map is copyright, so none is used here; if you like, bring one to class and ask the same question of it (what is joined to what, and what the map leaves out). The one idea: a network diagram keeps connections and drops the rest. Nodes are the things (stations), edges are the joins (lines). Degree is the number of edges that meet at a node. The sum of all the degrees is twice the number of edges, because every edge has two ends; this is used in the next lesson. Line length on a diagram like this is just what fits on the page. Mermaid, which draws the map, places boxes by its own layout rules, which is a useful point to make: the same network can be drawn many ways. Wider idea: "connected" means you can follow edges from any node to any other. Marina (degree 0) is the first example of a node that isn't. Edge weights (distances or times) come later. running: - "Opening: ask which stations they pass on the way from Fernbank to Hilltop before they see Predict." - "Predict: take a show of hands before the answer is shown. Those who pick Market to Hilltop are reading the line length as a distance." - "Paper: the degree try-one after the worked example and the Make task are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for a sketch with dots and lines." - "Modify: ask for Marina's degree before students type it. Zero is an answer." stuck: - see: A student says Hilltop is the furthest because its line is the longest. ask: If I redraw the map with that line shorter, did the train get faster? fix: Length on the page isn't length of the ride. The map only says the stations are joined. - see: A student gives Quay's degree as 4 (counting Quay itself) or counts the stations. ask: Count the lines at Quay, not the stations. fix: "Degree is the number of edges that meet there. Quay has three: to Fernbank, Market and Park." - see: A student says Marina isn't on the map, so it has no degree. ask: Is Marina a node? fix: It is a node, with degree 0. stretch: Draw the same network a different way, with different line lengths. Does anything the map tells you change? support: Give students the map printed with each node coloured in as they count its edges. leads: > Starts AC9M10SP02. Where it leads: following paths and asking whether every edge can be used once (Every street once), then polyhedra as networks (Euler's rule). exit: q: A network has 9 edges. What do the degrees of all its nodes add up to? a: "18." explain: > A **network** is nodes joined by edges. A map of train lines is a network: the stations are nodes and the lines are edges. The **degree** of a node is how many edges meet there. A network keeps only who is joined to whom, so the length of a line on the page isn't a distance. ```

# Lena's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: lena
The map has a line from Market to Hilltop and a line from Fernbank to Quay.
On the page, the Market to Hilltop line is three times as long.
So the ride from Market to Hilltop is three times as long.
So the ride to Hilltop takes longest.
# endregion
